draft.title: How monetary policy works
card: When the RBA changes the cash rate, banks usually change the interest rates they charge on loans and pay on deposits. This is the first step in how the change spreads through the economy.
A higher cash rate tends to lift the Australian dollar, because higher returns attract foreign funds. It also tends to lower asset prices, such as shares and housing, as borrowing costs more.
These changes alter spending. Higher rates make borrowing dearer and saving more rewarding, so households and firms tend to spend and invest less. Lower rates tend to do the opposite.
Spending changes demand, which affects inflation. The full effect usually takes one to two years to show.
draft.remember: A cash rate change passes through interest rates, the dollar and asset prices to spending, then inflation.

a.q: The RBA raises the cash rate. Which is the most likely effect on household spending?
opts: It falls, because borrowing costs more and saving pays more
It rises, because the dollar becomes cheaper for buyers
It falls, because banks stop lending to all households
It stays the same, as the effect is only on inflation
a.why: Higher loan rates and better deposit returns make households spend less. The dollar usually rises, not falls, after a rate rise, so the second option has the effect backwards.
a.clue: Think about what a higher loan rate does to borrowers.

b.q: The RBA cuts the cash rate. Mia, who runs a café in Dubbo, has a business loan. Which describes the chain of effects that could follow?
opts: Loan rates fall, spending rises, inflation pressure grows
Loan rates fall, spending rises, inflation pressure eases
Loan rates rise, spending falls, inflation pressure eases
Loan rates fall, spending falls, inflation pressure grows
b.why: A cut lowers loan rates, so borrowing and spending tend to rise. More demand adds to inflation pressure. The second option has the right first steps but gets the final effect on inflation wrong.
b.clue: More spending means more demand in the economy.

a.best: It falls, because borrowing costs more and saving pays more

b.best: Loan rates fall, spending rises, inflation pressure grows
